I think about why the event has happened to me
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette: The rollover on the winding county road happened on a Tuesday. Elias had been driving home from a location scout when the asphalt slicked with sudden rain, the tires lost their grip, and the world inverted. He was trapped in the twisted cabin as the engine sputtered into silence, swallowed by a darkness so complete it pressed against his eyes. Metal groaned, glass settled, and when the emergency crews finally pried the door, their flashlights cut through the wreckage in harsh, overlapping beams. He survived, but the event refused to settle into a narrative. What remained were frames: the exact angle of the steering column buckling inward, the way the emergency lights caught the dust hanging in the air, the precise geometry of cracked window glass. He tried to explain it to Clara over tea, but the words dissolved the moment they reached his tongue. He simply shook his head, certain that the accident could not be spoken, only seen. Over the following weeks, his daily rhythm shifted. He found himself sitting near the edge of his studio office chair, eyes constantly scanning the doorways, watching the periphery of every room he entered. A dropped set of keys made him lurch backward, his heart hammering against his ribs. He was on high alert for any sudden noise, his shoulders tightening the moment a monitor whirred to life or a production assistant called out across the soundstage. His startle response left him pale and breathless long after the noise had passed. The visuals played on loop behind his eyelids during storyboards, crisp and unyielding, refusing to soften into memory. He avoided unlit corridors at the editing facility and refused night shoots. He spent his evenings asking himself why he had been the one to survive. He also found himself occupying his mind with anything else: counting coiled cables, running diagnostics on camera bodies, memorizing call sheets. His perception of threat in sounds operated alongside his preference for unlit spaces. The darkness of the production offices felt identical to the cabin. He looked at his old directing journals, at the steady cadence he used to bring to a set, and felt a quiet certainty that he was inadequate. The way he flinched at a clapperboard, the way he couldn't sit through a dinner without watching the windows, were constant reminders of his daily reality. Clara noticed the distance. He canceled a weekend getaway, let rehearsals run late, and stopped attending premieres, his absence a quiet subtraction from their shared life. When she asked if he was struggling, he just touched his own forearm, unable to translate the knot in his chest into language. He was certain that his reactions proved he was a lousy coper, that the person he had become was unrecognizable to everyone around him, including himself. The visual recall and the sound sensitivities occupied his days without merging. His avoidance of dark sets, his habit of searching for meaning, and his tendency to distract himself were parallel rhythms. Now, at fifty-two, Elias booked an intake session. What finally brought him to the clinic was a night shoot on an industrial lot where a generator cut out for four seconds. The sudden silence made his chest clamp shut, and it took until the backup engines roared to life before he could stand. He is exhausted from the constant vigilance, the way his hands won't stop checking door handles, the hollow space where his certainty used to live. He hopes someone can help him quiet the fragmented images and the watching, not because he wants a tidy explanation, but because he is desperate to stop feeling like a stranger in his own days.
